Triggers.value: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure

Maladaptive Strategies.value: rehearse what to say before any interaction
cut off all contact with friends and family

Memory.value: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Negative Appraisals.value: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me
I can no longer trust my own body

issues.item: Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military
issues.explanation: Military-themed conversations are hard to reconcile with a life-threatening illness trauma in a 51-year-old school principal; this trigger implies a combat-related context not represented anywhere else in the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar People: Seeing other people that were involved in the event or that look similar
issues.explanation: Avoiding people involved in the event or who look similar fits interpersonal/assault/accident traumas better than life-threatening illness, where there are typically no 'other people involved' in that sense. It is not well supported by the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Future Orientation: Talking about the future
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening illness trauma, 'talking about the future' as a trigger is plausible, but 'alcohol smell' is hard to connect unless alcohol was part of treatment context; nothing else in the profile supports that association, making this trigger set clinically incoherent.

'People can't be trusted' is more typical of interpersonal trauma and is poorly anchored to a life-threatening illness trauma in the absence of any treatment-related betrayal, conflict, or mistrust themes elsewhere in the profile.

'Crying' is not a trauma cue but an affective response/behavior, so it is clinically incoherent as a trigger item relative to the other trigger items, which are concrete sensory reminders linked to life-threatening illness (alcohol smell, hospital/antiseptic smell).

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: A global mistrust appraisal is a poor fit for the rest of the profile and trauma type. In life-threatening illness, the other items center on altered self and self-reliance, while 'People can't be trusted' implies an interpersonal betrayal/threat theme that is not supported by the memory, trigger, or strategy items and does not align well with the otherwise weak/inactive Threat links.

vignette: Arthur Vance had been thirty-nine when his body suddenly turned against him. Reviewing budget allocations in his principal's office, he felt a cold, crushing weight seize his chest before collapsing. The emergency response unfolded in fragments that refused to cohere. He remembered the sharp sting of alcohol prep pads against his forearm during a central line insertion, the heavy hiss of a ventilator that made his own breath feel like a violation, and the rigid posture of his hospital bed, knees bent, arms pinned. When he woke, the memories remained stubbornly out of reach. He could not deliberately piece them together; instead, a raw panic would rise in his throat, accompanied by the exact physical tension of that bed, as if his limbs were still bound. Over the following months, Arthur's life narrowed to avoid threatening cues. He began rehearsing every conversation beforehand, mapping out syllables in the shower, terrified that a single unscripted word would expose a profound fragility. He stopped returning calls, telling himself he needed quiet, though he had come to believe his own body was no longer trustworthy. He avoided the district's annual wellness screenings, finding that the mere prospect of undergoing a medical examination or procedure triggered immediate, paralyzing dread. When he drove past the local clinic, he turned away when the scent of antiseptic from its ventilation system filled his car. His daily environment, once a place of routine leadership, became a landscape of potential contamination. The triggers manifested with brutal specificity. At a district leadership dinner, when a colleague uncorked a bottle of scotch, the sharp aroma of alcohol rolled across the table. Arthur felt his diaphragm lock, instantly transported back to the chemical sterility of the ICU. He left mid-sentence, claiming a migraine. At school, he avoided the administrative wing where the cleaning crew's industrial disinfectants mirrored the hospital smell that once signaled his deepest helplessness. He stopped attending faculty breakfasts, isolating completely from colleagues he had once mentored. He was certain that his unrecognizable self-a man who could not rely on himself to lead or steady his own breathing-would be exposed if he stayed. Now, at fifty-one and widowed, Arthur sat on the edge of a referral form. His wife had passed two years prior, leaving him alone with his daily retreats. He had come to the clinic because the rehearsing had exhausted him, and the silence from his former staff had turned into a heavy, isolating weight. He was most afraid that his body would fail him again without warning, leaving him powerless. What he hoped for was a way to stop bracing for collapse, to trust that a familiar scent no longer meant danger. He sat ready to speak, not because he remembered the illness clearly, but because the emotion without an image had finally become too loud to carry alone.
